run.question: Density of Kepler-139 d?
run.answer: The density of Kepler-139 d computed from its default parameter set is 5.29 g/cm3, with a 16th-84th percentile range of 3.05 to 7.69 g/cm3. These planetary values come from Weiss et al. 2024 [pset-kepler-139-d-weiss-et-al-2024], following the single-source consistency rules outlined in kb:derived_quantities. Because the archive mass is a minimum mass (M*sin(i)), this density is a lower limit.

A derived quantity must be computed from inputs that all come from one published parameter set. Where a default set and a composite value disagree, the self-consistent single-source set governs. Planets are identified by catalogue designation. Sibling planets share a host star and must never have their parameters mixed.

Not in scope: population statistics, atmospheric composition, and any parameter without a citable published source.

# Derived Quantities: Density, Teq, Insolation, HZ

Formulas and methodology for computing density, equilibrium temperature, insolation flux, and habitable-zone assessment; requirement that inputs share a single parameter set

All derived quantities in this knowledge base must be computed from inputs drawn from a single, self-consistent published parameter set. Mixing values from different papers (e.g., using a radius from one study and a mass from another) produces a result that is not self-consistent and must be labelled as a composite alternative, never presented as the primary answer. For how the NASA Exoplanet Archive constructs its composite (mixed-provenance) PSCompPars table, see `composite_parameters`; for tracing any value to its source paper, see `parameter_provenance`.

## Planet Density ρ_p

When both planetary radius R_p and planetary mass M_p are available from the **same** parameter set, density is calculated assuming a spherical planet [1]:

$$\rho_p = \frac{3 M_p}{4\pi R_p^3}$$

The archive calculates this value only when it is not already empirically reported, and does not report uncertainties on calculated values [1].

## Planet Equilibrium Temperature T_eq

Requires stellar radius R_★, stellar effective temperature T_eff, and orbital semi-major axis a — all from the same parameter set [1]:

$$T_{eq} = T_{\star} \sqrt{\frac{R_{\star}}{a}} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/4}$$

R_★ and a must be in the same units (both converted to km using IAU standards) [1]. This formula assumes zero albedo and efficient heat redistribution. No uncertainty is reported on the calculated result.

## Planet Insolation Flux S

Requires stellar luminosity L_★ and semi-major axis a [1]:

$$\frac{S}{S_{\oplus}} = \left(\frac{L_{\star}}{L_{\odot}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{AU}}{a}\right)^2$$

If L_★ is not empirically available but R_★ and T_eff are, the archive first calculates L_★ via the Stefan-Boltzmann law [1]:

$$L_{\star} = 4\pi R_{\star}^{2}\, \sigma\, T_{\mathrm{eff}}^{4}$$

Both L_★ inputs must originate from the same parameter set as a to preserve self-consistency.

## Stellar Luminosity L_★ (intermediate derived value)

Calculated from R_★ and T_eff using the Stefan-Boltzmann law (formula above) when an empirical L_★ is not available [1]. This intermediate is then used in the insolation calculation.

## Habitable-Zone Assessment

Habitable-zone placement is evaluated using the insolation flux S/S_⊕ computed above. A planet's HZ status depends on which stellar and orbital inputs are used; switching parameter sets (e.g., using a revised stellar radius) changes S and therefore the HZ boundary comparison. Always confirm that R_★, T_eff, and a all come from the same published solution before reporting HZ status.

## Derived Planet Mass and Radius (when one is missing)

When a planet has an empirical radius but no empirical mass, or vice versa, the archive applies the Chen & Kipping (2017) mass–radius relation [1]:

**Radius from mass:**
$$\log_{10}(R_p/R_{\oplus}) = \mathcal{C} + \mathcal{S}\cdot\log_{10}(M_p/M_{\oplus})$$

**Mass from radius (inverse):**
$$\log_{10}(M_p/M_{\oplus}) = (\log_{10}(R_p/R_{\oplus}) - \mathcal{C})\,/\,\mathcal{S}$$

The piecewise coefficients {C; S} from Chen & Kipping (2017) Table 2 used by the archive are [1]:

| Mass regime | C | S |
|---|---|---|
| M_p < 2.04 M_⊕ | 0.00346 | 0.2790 |
| (higher regimes) | (per C&K 2017) | (per C&K 2017) |

The third term of the mass-radius relation has a **negative slope**, so the radius-to-mass inversion uses a restricted set of coefficients to avoid unphysical results [1]. These mass/radius values are marked as "Calculated Value" in the archive's reference column, not attributed to a literature source.

## Key calculation rules (archive policy)

- A derived parameter is **not calculated** if any required input is a limit rather than a central value [1].
- **No uncertainties** are reported for any calculated parameter [1].
- The reference column for a calculated parameter reads **"Calculated Value"** [1].

When answering questions about a specific planet, confirm which parameter set supplies R_p, M_p, R_★, T_eff, and a. If values come from different papers, the derived quantities are composite estimates; identify them as such and note what a self-consistent single-source calculation would yield instead.

# Parameter Sets, Defaults, and Source Tracing

Which published parameter sets exist for a planet, how the archive picks a default set, and how to trace every value to its citable paper

Every confirmed planet in the NASA Exoplanet Archive has at least one published parameter set, and may have many. Understanding how sets are defined, selected as default, and traced to their source papers is essential before computing any derived quantity (density, insolation, equilibrium temperature, or habitable-zone position). Derived quantities must always be computed from a single, self-consistent parameter set (see composite_parameters for the PSCompPars alternative).

## What constitutes a parameter set

A parameter set is a coherent group of planet, stellar, and system values drawn from **a single peer-reviewed publication**. In the Planetary Systems (PS) table, each row represents exactly one such set for one planet: one row per planet per reference [1]. The `pl_refname` column (database name) identifies the publication backing the planet parameters in that row; individual parameters also carry their own `_reflink` columns (e.g., `pl_rade_reflink`, `pl_eqt_reflink`) pointing to the source of that specific value [2].

Parameters are ingested from two categories of source [1]:
- **Published peer-reviewed literature** — evaluated case-by-case by archive science staff.
- **NASA mission deliveries** — for Kepler Objects of Interest (KOIs) and TESS Objects of Interest; these appear with `soltype` = `Kepler Project Candidate` or `TESS Project Candidate` rather than `Published Confirmed`.

A new parameter set is ingested only if it **extends** (adds parameters not already held) or **improves** (higher precision, updated ephemerides) the existing holdings. Sets that do neither are not ingested, though the archive is responsive to community requests [1].

## Default parameter set selection

Every planet has exactly one parameter set flagged as default (`default_flag = 1` in the PS table) [2]. Archive science staff weigh three factors when choosing it [1]:

| Factor | Description |
|---|---|
| **Completeness** | How many planet parameters the set provides. A more complete single-source set reduces mixing when it feeds the PSCompPars table. |
| **Precision** | Quality of measurements; a paper may demonstrate improved precision despite larger formal uncertainties (e.g., by better modelling stellar variability). |
| **Large uniform surveys** | Re-analyses covering many planets simultaneously receive additional weight for their scientific utility as self-consistent catalogues. |

> **Important:** The default parameter set is not guaranteed to contain the most precise published value for any individual parameter. It is chosen for overall completeness and consistency [1].

The Transit and Ephemeris Service does **not** use the default set for its calculations; it uses whichever set has the most precise ephemeris [1].

## How to trace a value to its source paper

1. **Planetary Systems (PS) table** — filter on `default_flag = 1` for a one-row-per-planet view of default sets, or browse all rows to see every ingested parameter set. The `pl_refname` column identifies the publication for each row. Individual parameter reference columns (e.g., `pl_orbper_reflink`, `pl_rade_reflink`, `pl_eqt_reflink`, `pl_insol_reflink`, `pl_dens_reflink`) pin each value to its specific source [2].
2. **System Overview page** — click any planet name in the PS table to reach its System Overview. Expand the Stellar Parameters and Planetary Parameters sections (click the `+` signs) to view and compare all archived parameter sets side by side [1].
3. **`soltype` column** — distinguishes `Published Confirmed` (literature) from `Kepler Project Candidate` / `TESS Project Candidate` (mission pipeline) rows [2].
4. **`pl_controv_flag`** — set to `1` when the confirmation status of a planet has been questioned in the published literature [2].

## Why stellar parameters may differ across planets in the same system

The archive records the stellar parameters **used to derive the planetary parameters** for each row. If two planets in the same system come from different papers, their rows will carry the stellar values from their respective publications — those values may differ from each other [1]. This is expected behaviour, not an error: it preserves the self-consistency of each parameter set.

## Retracted and refuted planets

Confirmed planets later refuted in the literature receive a `False Positive Planet (FPP)` disposition. Their data remain on their System Overview pages (flagged as FPPs) but are removed from the PS and PSCompPars tables. Retracted objects are also listed on the Exoplanet Archive's Excluded Targets page [1].

## Key provenance columns at a glance

| Column | Table | What it records |
|---|---|---|
| `default_flag` | PS only | 1 = this row is the default parameter set for the planet |
| `pl_refname` | PS only | Publication backing the planet parameter row |
| `soltype` | PS only | Published Confirmed / Kepler Project Candidate / TESS Project Candidate |
| `pl_controv_flag` | PS + PSCompPars | 1 = confirmation status questioned in literature |
| `pl_bmassprov` | PS + PSCompPars | Provenance of best-mass estimate (Mass, M×sin(i)/sin(i), or M×sin(i)) |
| `*_reflink` | PS only | Per-parameter source reference (e.g., `pl_eqt_reflink`) |

For how the archive constructs a single filled-in row from multiple parameter sets, see composite_parameters.

run.question: Is TRAPPIST-1 e in the habitable zone?
run.answer: TRAPPIST-1 e is classified as inside the habitable zone with a probability inside of 0.963, calculated using the default parameter set from Agol et al. 2021 [pset-trappist-1-e-agol-et-al-2021] under single-source provenance rules kb:derived_quantities. Its incident insolation is 0.650 S_earth, with a 16th-84th percentile range of 0.546 to 0.781 S_earth. Because the host star's effective temperature of 2566 K is outside the 2600 to 7200 K fitting range of the habitable-zone model, the boundary limits are extrapolated.

Formulas and methodology for computing density, equilibrium temperature, insolation flux, and habitable-zone assessment; requirement that inputs share a single parameter set

All derived quantities in this knowledge base must be computed from inputs drawn from a single, self-consistent published parameter set. Mixing values from different papers (e.g., using a radius from one study and a mass from another) produces a result that is not self-consistent and must be labelled as a composite alternative, never presented as the primary answer. For how the NASA Exoplanet Archive constructs its composite (mixed-provenance) PSCompPars table, see `composite_parameters`; for tracing any value to its source paper, see `parameter_provenance`.

## Planet Density ρ_p

When both planetary radius R_p and planetary mass M_p are available from the **same** parameter set, density is calculated assuming a spherical planet [1]:

$$\rho_p = \frac{3 M_p}{4\pi R_p^3}$$

The archive calculates this value only when it is not already empirically reported, and does not report uncertainties on calculated values [1].

## Planet Equilibrium Temperature T_eq

Requires stellar radius R_★, stellar effective temperature T_eff, and orbital semi-major axis a — all from the same parameter set [1]:

$$T_{eq} = T_{\star} \sqrt{\frac{R_{\star}}{a}} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1/4}$$

R_★ and a must be in the same units (both converted to km using IAU standards) [1]. This formula assumes zero albedo and efficient heat redistribution. No uncertainty is reported on the calculated result.

## Planet Insolation Flux S

Requires stellar luminosity L_★ and semi-major axis a [1]:

$$\frac{S}{S_{\oplus}} = \left(\frac{L_{\star}}{L_{\odot}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{AU}}{a}\right)^2$$

If L_★ is not empirically available but R_★ and T_eff are, the archive first calculates L_★ via the Stefan-Boltzmann law [1]:

$$L_{\star} = 4\pi R_{\star}^{2}\, \sigma\, T_{\mathrm{eff}}^{4}$$

Both L_★ inputs must originate from the same parameter set as a to preserve self-consistency.

## Stellar Luminosity L_★ (intermediate derived value)

Calculated from R_★ and T_eff using the Stefan-Boltzmann law (formula above) when an empirical L_★ is not available [1]. This intermediate is then used in the insolation calculation.

## Habitable-Zone Assessment

Habitable-zone placement is evaluated using the insolation flux S/S_⊕ computed above. A planet's HZ status depends on which stellar and orbital inputs are used; switching parameter sets (e.g., using a revised stellar radius) changes S and therefore the HZ boundary comparison. Always confirm that R_★, T_eff, and a all come from the same published solution before reporting HZ status.

## Derived Planet Mass and Radius (when one is missing)

When a planet has an empirical radius but no empirical mass, or vice versa, the archive applies the Chen & Kipping (2017) mass–radius relation [1]:

**Radius from mass:**
$$\log_{10}(R_p/R_{\oplus}) = \mathcal{C} + \mathcal{S}\cdot\log_{10}(M_p/M_{\oplus})$$

**Mass from radius (inverse):**
$$\log_{10}(M_p/M_{\oplus}) = (\log_{10}(R_p/R_{\oplus}) - \mathcal{C})\,/\,\mathcal{S}$$

The piecewise coefficients {C; S} from Chen & Kipping (2017) Table 2 used by the archive are [1]:

| Mass regime | C | S |
|---|---|---|
| M_p < 2.04 M_⊕ | 0.00346 | 0.2790 |
| (higher regimes) | (per C&K 2017) | (per C&K 2017) |

The third term of the mass-radius relation has a **negative slope**, so the radius-to-mass inversion uses a restricted set of coefficients to avoid unphysical results [1]. These mass/radius values are marked as "Calculated Value" in the archive's reference column, not attributed to a literature source.

## Key calculation rules (archive policy)

- A derived parameter is **not calculated** if any required input is a limit rather than a central value [1].
- **No uncertainties** are reported for any calculated parameter [1].
- The reference column for a calculated parameter reads **"Calculated Value"** [1].

When answering questions about a specific planet, confirm which parameter set supplies R_p, M_p, R_★, T_eff, and a. # Parameter Sets, Defaults, and Source Tracing

## What constitutes a parameter set

A parameter set is a coherent group of planet, stellar, and system values drawn from **a single peer-reviewed publication**. ## Default parameter set selection

Every planet has exactly one parameter set flagged as default (`default_flag = 1` in the PS table) [2]. Archive science staff weigh three factors when choosing it [1]:

| Factor | Description |
|---|---|
| **Completeness** | How many planet parameters the set provides. A more complete single-source set reduces mixing when it feeds the PSCompPars table. |
| **Precision** | Quality of measurements; a paper may demonstrate improved precision despite larger formal uncertainties (e.g., by better modelling stellar variability). |
| **Large uniform surveys** | Re-analyses covering many planets simultaneously receive additional weight for their scientific utility as self-consistent catalogues. |
